First, we substitute $u={x}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u={x}^{3}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{2}^{u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{2}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{{2}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }[{2}^{u}]_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{2}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y={2}^{a},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{a}=0$

- ${lim}_{a\to \infty }{2}^{a}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/b9a29cbd8a029e0f26e3da6a042ada0f8a809053233979bb4ff73db3dcf0f10d.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{x}^{2}\cdot {2}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$
